ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating KL-Regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Experiment with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) to fine-tune a pre-trained diffusion model for the task of image-to-image translation on the Style Transfer dataset from DALL-E 2, while incorporating a KL-regularization term that approximates the marginal KL divergence using trajectories generated by the model. Evaluate fine-tuned models using metrics such as Inception Score (IS) and Fréchet Inception Distance (FID).
CONTROLS: Compare against the original pre-trained model, a version of PPO without KL regularization, and a best-of-N sampling baseline.
COST: 1620
PREDICTION: Fine-tuned models with KL regularization show a 10-20% improvement in IS and FID scores, but may suffer from instability if the regularization term is too strong, leading to a failure to converge.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Investigating Multi-Step Fine-Tuning for Flow Models
PROPOSAL: Design a new algorithm that fine-tunes a pre-trained flow model for molecule generation using a trajectory-based KL regularization, where the regularization term is computed as the KL divergence between the denoising trajectories of the pre-trained model and the fine-tuned model. Perform multiple fine-tuning steps, where each step refines the model based on the previous denoising trajectories and the reward signal. Evaluate the performance of the fine-tuned model on molecule generation benchmarks such as QM9 and ZINC.
CONTROLS: Compare against a single-step PPO algorithm, a best-of-N sampling baseline, and the original pre-trained flow model.
COST: 4500
PREDICTION: The multi-step fine-tuning algorithm shows a significant improvement (25-40%) in molecule generation metrics such as RMSD and MAE, but may require a larger number of fine-tuning steps to converge, leading to a potential failure in terms of computational cost.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Investigating Rejection Sampling for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Adapt the rejection sampling framework for autoregressive models to diffusion models, using the pre-trained model as the proposal distribution and the reward signal as the acceptance criterion. Evaluate the performance of the rejection sampling algorithm on text-to-image generation benchmarks such as MSCOCO and LVIS, comparing against a PPO baseline and the original pre-trained model.
CONTROLS: Compare against a best-of-N sampling baseline and a PPO algorithm without KL regularization.
COST: 2700
PREDICTION: The rejection sampling algorithm shows a 20-30% improvement in metrics such as BLEU and Inception Score, but may suffer from mode collapse if the proposal distribution is too concentrated, leading to a failure to capture the full range of rewards.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Investigating Rejection Sampling for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Modify the rejection sampling algorithm to incorporate a weighted sampling scheme, where the weights are computed based on the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the proposal distribution and the reward signal. This allows the algorithm to adapt to the changing proposal distribution during training. Evaluate the performance of the weighted rejection sampling algorithm on text-to-image generation benchmarks such as MSCOCO and LVIS.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original rejection sampling algorithm, a PPO baseline, and the original pre-trained model.
COST: 3240
PREDICTION: The weighted rejection sampling algorithm shows a 30-40% improvement in metrics such as BLEU and Inception Score, by better adapting to the changing proposal distribution, but may suffer from increased computational cost due to the weighting scheme.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Investigating Best-of-N Sampling for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Extend the best-of-N sampling framework for autoregressive models to diffusion models, using the pre-trained model as the proposal distribution and selecting the top-N samples based on the reward signal. Evaluate the performance of the best-of-N sampling algorithm on document layout generation benchmarks such as Dataset9 and IIIT-Dataset, comparing against a PPO baseline and the original pre-trained model.
CONTROLS: Compare against a rejection sampling baseline and a PPO algorithm without KL regularization.
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: The best-of-N sampling algorithm shows a 25-35% improvement in metrics such as F-score and Inception Score, by selecting the most rewarded samples, but may suffer from increased computational cost due to the need to evaluate multiple samples per iteration.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Investigating Zero-Shot Fine-Tuning of Flow Models
PROPOSAL: Explore the possibility of zero-shot fine-tuning of pre-trained flow models using only samples from the data distribution, without any explicit reward signal or additional training data. Evaluate the performance of the fine-tuned model on molecule generation benchmarks such as QM9 and ZINC, comparing against a PPO baseline and the original pre-trained flow model.
CONTROLS: Compare against a version of the PPO algorithm that uses a noisy reward signal and a version that uses a randomly initialized flow model.
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: The zero-shot fine-tuning algorithm shows a 15-25% improvement in metrics such as RMSD and MAE, by correcting for errors in the pre-trained model, but may suffer from mode collapse due to the lack of explicit reward signal, leading to a need for careful hyperparameter tuning.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating KL-Regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Modify the KL-regularized reward maximization algorithm to use a more robust estimator of the marginal KL divergence between the pre-trained model and the fine-tuned model, which accounts for the multi-step structure of the diffusion process. Evaluate the performance of the modified algorithm on image-to-image translation benchmarks such as Style Transfer, comparing against a PPO baseline and the original pre-trained model.
CONTROLS: Compare against a version of the algorithm that uses a standard estimator of the marginal KL divergence and a version that uses the original rejection sampling baseline as a finer regularization term.
COST: 8025
PREDICTION: The modified KL-regularized reward maximization algorithm shows a 20-30% improvement in metrics such as Inception Score and Fréchet Inception Distance, by better accounting for the multi-step structure of the diffusion process, but may suffer from increased computational cost due to the more complex KL divergence estimator.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Denoising Trajectory Regularization
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effects of adding regularization terms to the fine-tuning objective that directly penalize the denoising trajectories of the diffusion model, rather than relying on KL-regularization or other indirect methods. Evaluate the performance of the modified fine-tuning algorithm on text-to-image generation benchmarks such as MSCOCO and LVIS, comparing against a PPO baseline and the original pre-trained model.
CONTROLS: Compare against a version of the algorithm that uses standard PPO without any regularization terms and a version that uses a randomly selected set of regularization terms.
COST: 9000
PREDICTION: The denoising trajectory regularization shows a 10-20% improvement in metrics such as Inception Score and BLEU, by directly penalizing denoising trajectories that deviate from the target data distribution, but may suffer from mode collapse or oscillations in the fine-tuned model due to the lack of a global objective function.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Fine-Tuning Algorithms to Dataset Shift
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness of the fine-tuning algorithms developed in this research to out-of-distribution (OOD) data, by evaluating the performance of the fine-tuned models on datasets that are similar to but not identical to the training data. Evaluate the performance of the fine-tuned models on OOD datasets such as ImageNet and CIFAR-10, comparing against a PPO baseline and the original pre-trained model.
CONTROLS: Compare against a version of the algorithm that uses a different set of OOD datasets and a version that uses a single OOD dataset.
COST: 12750
PREDICTION: The fine-tuning algorithms show a significant drop in performance on OOD datasets, by a factor of 2-5, due to the lack of robustness to dataset shift, but the exact magnitude of the drop may depend on the specific algorithm and the characteristics of the OOD datasets.

ACTION: REVISE 7
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Fine-Tuning Algorithms to Dataset Shift
PROPOSAL: Modify the evaluation protocol for the robustness of fine-tuning algorithms to out-of-distribution (OOD) data to include a more nuanced set of OOD datasets, such as ImageNet and CIFAR-10 with varying degrees of similarity to the training data. Additionally, evaluate the robustness of the fine-tuning algorithms to different types of OOD data, such as OOD classes, OOD generation parameters, and OOD data distributions. Evaluate the performance of the fine-tuned models on these OOD datasets, comparing against a PPO baseline and the original pre-trained model.
CONTROLS: Compare against a version of the algorithm that uses a standard evaluation protocol and a version that uses a different set of OOD datasets.
COST: 15300
PREDICTION: The modified fine-tuning algorithms show a significant drop in performance on OOD datasets, by a factor of 2-5, but the drop appears to be more nuanced and dependent on the specific characteristics of the OOD data, rather than a fixed factor.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating KL-regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Design a synthetic experiment comparing KL-regularized PPO with and without KL regularization, using the 3D-WCDATA dataset, and measuring the effect of KL regularization on model stability and reward maximization on a simple text-to-image generation task.
CONTROLS: PPO without KL regularization, standard PPO using only the reward signal
COST: 30
PREDICTION: KL-regularization should improve model stability but may not significantly improve reward maximization, potentially due to the suboptimal trajectory KL relaxation used in practice.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Characterizing KL Regret in Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Develop a theoretical analysis of the KL regret incurred by fine-tuning diffusion models under KL-regularized PPO, within the regime of mild weight perturbations and small reward fluctuations. We assume access to a lower bound on the KL divergence, obtained by upper-bounding the trajectory KL divergence.
CONTROLS: - None required, as this is a theoretical result
COST: 90
PREDICTION: The analysis will reveal a lower bound on the asymptotic KL regret that involves the product of the reward and the square root of the KL divergence between the pre-trained and target distributions, which will guide the design of effective fine-tuning algorithms.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Comparing Fine-Tuning Methods for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Design an experiment comparing the performance of KL-regularized PPO, rejection sampling, and best-of-N sampling for fine-tuning diffusion models on real-world benchmarks in text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation. We will measure fine-tuning speed, reward maximization, and sample quality.
CONTROLS: KL-regularized PPO with and without KL regularization, rejection sampling without fine-tuning, a baseline diffusion model without fine-tuning
COST: 150
PREDICTION: Rejection sampling will outperform KL-regularized PPO for fine-tuning speed, while KL-regularized PPO will yield better rewards, and best-of-N sampling might perform poorly due to its inefficiencies.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Exploiting Generative Structure for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether conditioning fine-tuning on intermediate variables from the diffusion chain improves fine-tuning performance. We will conduct an experiment on a text-to-image generation task using a diffusion model based on the DDPM architecture, and compare the performance of fine-tuning directly on the model's output versus conditioning on intermediate noise schedules and denoised images.
CONTROLS: KL-regularized PPO with and without conditioning on intermediate variables, rejection sampling without fine-tuning
COST: 110
PREDICTION: Conditioning on intermediate variables will yield significantly better rewards and sample quality, especially when combined with KL-regularized PPO, due to the exploitation of the model's generative structure.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Rev. Characterizing KL Regret in Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Strengthen the theoretical analysis by deriving a sharp bound on the KL regret, involving the expectation of the reward and the square root of the KL divergence between the pre-trained and target distributions, under the assumption of a fixed enough reward signal. Additionally, explore the use of multi-step functional contraction arguments to derive a better convergence rate.
CONTROLS: - None required, as this is a theoretical result
COST: 130
PREDICTION: The sharp bound will cover a wider range of reward signals and provide a more accurate estimate of the KL regret, allowing for more informed design of fine-tuning algorithms.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Flow-based Fine-Tuning without Reward
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether the discrepancies between a pre-trained flow model and the target data distribution can be corrected without explicit reward feedback. We will design an experiment using a mixture-of-experts flow model, and aim to correct the discrepancies through multi-sample importance weighting and learned perturbations of the flow.
CONTROLS: Pre-trained flow model with no fine-tuning, the same model fine-tuned with an explicit reward signal
COST: 140
PREDICTION: The experiment will show that importance weighting and learned perturbations can correct for moderate discrepancies between the pre-trained model and the target distribution, but significantly increasing discrepancies may hinder accurate correction due to the limited capacity of the model.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Weakly-supervised Fine-Tuning of Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether a weakly-supervised learning scheme, where the fine-tuning loss is a combination of the KL regularized objective and a least-squares matching loss between the pre-trained and fine-tuned diffusion distributions, can achieve better sample quality and reward maximization than fully-supervised approaches.
CONTROLS: KL-regularized PPO, rejection sampling, and the flow-based fine-tuning without reward, with and without the weakly-supervised loss term
COST: 160
PREDICTION: The experiment will show that weakly-supervised learning can achieve significantly better sample quality and reward maximization than fully-supervised approaches, especially in scenarios where data is scarce or annotation is challenging.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Divergence-based Confidence Estimates for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Develop a technique to estimate the confidence of generated samples from diffusion models using divergence-based metrics (e.g., KL, JS, or Wasserstein distances) between the pre-trained and fine-tuned distributions. This can be used as a regularization term in the fine-tuning objective or to filter high-confidence samples.
CONTROLS: KL-regularized PPO, rejection sampling, and the flow-based fine-tuning without reward, with and without the confidence term
COST: 180
PREDICTION: The divergence-based confidence estimates will provide a reliable indicator of sample quality, enabling better selection of high-confidence samples and aiding in fine-tuning by guiding the algorithm towards a more confident and well-calibrated distribution.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Sampling for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Design an adaptive sampling strategy that balances exploration and exploitation by selecting samples based on the uncertainty of the model and the divergence-based confidence estimates developed in Proposal 7. We will show that this approach can improve fine-tuning convergence rates and achieve better sample quality.
CONTROLS: KL-regularized PPO, rejection sampling, and the flow-based fine-tuning without reward, with and without the adaptive sampling strategy
COST: 200
PREDICTION: The uncertainty-aware adaptive sampling will significantly reduce convergence times and improve sample quality, while also providing a more robust and flexible framework for fine-tuning diffusion models, especially in complex and high-dimensional domains.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Rev. Flow-based Fine-Tuning without Reward
PROPOSAL: Strengthen the theoretical foundation for flow-based fine-tuning without reward by developing a convergence analysis for the iterative importance weighting and learned perturbation updates. We will also explore the use of entropy regularization to encourage exploration of the target distribution.
CONTROLS: The same experiments as before, but with an additional analysis of the convergence and exploratory properties of the revised method.
COST: 220
PREDICTION: The convergence analysis will reveal that importance weighting and learned perturbations can converge to the target distribution even without explicit reward feedback, but the speed and accuracy of convergence may depend on the choice of parameters, regularization, and exploration strategies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fine-tuning diffusion models with mixtures of conditional and marginal likelihoods
PROPOSAL: We propose to alleviate the issue of intractable marginal likelihoods by incorporating a mixture of conditional and marginal likelihoods, either through an auxiliary language model trained on the data distribution or through a sequence of discerning samples used to approximate the marginal through combination of unconditional one-step denoising likelihoods. This allows us to regularize the fine-tuned distribution with respect to a tractable marginal KL divergence and select informative guides for fine-tuning. The mixture weights and conditional probabilities for marginal adaptation are learned simultaneously and jointly, thus learning to balance both KL regularized reward maximization and density matching in a single step.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments with a standard KL-regularized PPO implementation that either ignores the KL term (as done in practice for diffusion models) or use an upper-bounding approximation, as well as ablations of the proposed mixture components such as different types of guides (e.g., language models, random samples, etc.).
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: Expected results are a reduction in overfitting and improvement in reward-aligned samples compared to current KL-ignoring strategies. However, adaptability and flexibility in incorporating both KL regularization and marginal adaptation may lead to initial instability in learning the optimal balance of both components.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Leverage task-specific prior knowledge for KL-regularized reward maximization
PROPOSAL: Inspired by techniques such as meta-learning and task-specific reward learning, we propose to incorporate task-specific prior knowledge into the KL-regularized reward maximization objective. Specifically, we use a task-specific prior distribution, learned only once per task, to enforce the learned reverse process to produce samples that are not only rewarded but also close to the task-specific distribution. This greatly alleviates the issue of the initial value function bias problem and leads to faster adaptation.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments with standard KL-regularized PPO implementation that either ignores the KL term or uses an upper-bounding approximation, as well as ablations of the proposed task-specific prior, e.g., without the prior or using a generic prior.
COST: 4320
PREDICTION: Expect a significant reduction in adaptation time and improvement in fine-tuned sample quality, especially in low-reward regions. However, proper initialization of the task-specific prior may require tuning, potentially introducing additional computational cost.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Fine-tuning diffusion models with mixtures of conditional and marginal likelihoods
PROPOSAL: Revised to: Incorporating Stochastic Path Information for Fine-tuning Diffusion Models. We modify the original proposal by using stochastic path information obtained from the intermediate denoising steps. Instead of relying solely on the mean-field estimates, we incorporate the variability and inter-sample correlations from the intermediate denoising steps by conditioning on the learned intermediate representations of high-reward samples. This allows us to better leverage the structure of the diffusion process and improve fine-tuned sample quality.
CONTROLS: Same as before, with additional experiments on different intermediate representation choices and stochastic path metrics (e.g., KL-divergence, Inception Score).
COST: 4050 (revised down from previous estimate considering the modification)
PREDICTION: Expect better alignment with the target distribution and improved reward maximization, leveraging the rich structure of the diffusion model. However, principled selection of intermediate representations and suitable stochastic path metrics may require additional tuning and hyperparameter search.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Leveraging flow model structure to alleviate the initial value function bias
PROPOSES: Inspired by the mathematical structure of flow models, we propose to decompose the KL regularization into a sum of respective KL divergences over each flow step. This decomposition allows us to independently regularize each flow step, reducing the dependency on an accurate initialization of the entire reverse process. By minimizing the KL divergence for each flow step separately, we alleviate the initial value function bias problem, enabling more effective fine-tuning of flow models.
CONTROLS: Comparison to the standard KL-regularized PPO implementation using an upper-bounding approximation, control experiments on importance weight schedules and the impact of the decomposition on the reverse process initialization, and diagnostic analysis on the relative contributions of each flow step to the overall KL regularization.
COST: 6480
PREDICTION: Expected results include reduced initial value function bias and better adaptation of flow models to the target distribution. However, the choice of KL regularizers for each flow step may require careful tuning and selection.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial fine-tuning to correct discretization and statistical errors
PROPOSAL: Given that diffusion and flow models can generate samples that slightly deviate from the data distribution due to discretization and statistical errors, we propose an adversarial fine-tuning approach. The idea is to train a discriminator that can differentiate between generated samples and real samples from the target data distribution. We then fine-tune the diffusion or flow model to produce samples that are more similar to the real samples as measured by the discriminator. This approach corrects errors without explicit reward and leverages the structure of the diffusion or flow model to achieve better sample quality at a reasonable cost in generation compute.
CONTROLS: Comparison to a standard KL-regularized PPO implementation using an upper-bounding approximation and ablation studies on different discriminator architectures and fine-tuning objectives.
COST: 5040
PREDICTION: Expected results include improved sample quality, especially in regions of the data distribution where the pre-trained model exhibits errors. The choice of discriminator and fine-tuning objectives may require careful tuning and selection.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Rejection sampling for efficient fine-tuning of diffusion models
PROPOSAL: Building on the idea of rejection sampling, we propose a modified version that selectively adapts to the reward function and pre-trained model's structure. By maintaining a buffer of high-reward samples, we can efficiently fine-tune the diffusion model, focusing on regions of the data distribution that are relevant for the task at hand. This allows for faster adaptation, reduced computational cost, and preservation of the sample quality.
CONTROLS: Comparison to standard KL-regularized PPO implementation using an upper-bounding approximation and ablation studies on different buffer sizes, sampling strategies, and tie-in with flow model structure.
COST: 6048
PREDICTION: Expected results include faster adaptation and improved fine-tuned sample quality, particularly in regions of the data distribution relevant to the task. However, the calibration of buffer size and sampling strategy may require careful tuning to avoid suboptimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Best-of-N sampling for transferable and efficient fine-tuning of diffusion models
PROPOSAL: Drawing inspiration from methods such as Best-of-N sampling and its connections to policy gradient methods, we propose to fine-tune diffusion models by sampling multiple trajectories from the model, evaluating them with respect to the reward function, and then selecting the best-performing trajectories to fine-tune the model. This approach promotes transferability across different tasks and samples by maintaining the diversity of samples while focusing on high-reward regions. It also encourages the model to adapt to the structure of the diffusion process and improves sample quality.
CONTROLS: Comparison to standard KL-regularized PPO implementation using an upper-bounding approximation and ablation studies on different sampling schemes, Best-of-N retrieval strategies (e.g., majority voting, argmax), and fine-tuning rates.
COST: 6720
PREDICTION: Expected results include improved transferability and faster adaptation to new tasks, due to the promoted diversity of samples and fine-tuned focusing on high-reward regions. The effectiveness of the approach depends on the choice of sampling schemes and Best-of-N retrieval strategies.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Best-of-N sampling for transferable and efficient fine-tuning of diffusion models
PROPOSAL: Revised to: Best-of-N sampling with adaptive noise schedules. Building on the previous proposal, we refine the Best-of-N sampling approach by introducing adaptive noise schedules. These schedules adjust the level of noise and exploration-exploitation tradeoff during the Best-of-N process, allowing the model to adapt to new tasks and sample distributions more effectively. By incorporating noise schedules learned from the task itself, we can promote better transferability and local minimization error correction.
CONTROLS: Comparison to standard KL-regularized PPO implementation using an upper-bounding approximation with and without adaptive noise schedules, ablation studies on different noise schedule learning algorithms and fine-tuning rates.
COST: 7200 (revised up to account for increased complexity and learning overhead)
PREDICTION: Expected results include improved transferability, reduced adaptation time for new tasks, and higher sample quality. The adaptation of noise schedules to new tasks may require careful tuning, potentially leading to over-adaptation and decreased robustness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Regularized flow-based KL-Divergence estimation for stricter regularized fine-tuning
PROPOSAL: Given the importance of accurate KL-divergence estimation in the regularized KL-regularized reward maximization objective, we propose to utilize a regularized flow-based method to efficiently approximate KL-divergence and improve fine-tuning sample quality. By leveraging the structure of the flow model, we can adapt the flow-based estimator to the pre-trained model's specific characteristics and optimize the estimation for each task, leading to more effective and regularized fine-tuning.
CONTROLS: Comparison to standard KL-regularized PPO implementation using an upper-bounding approximation with and without the flow-based KL estimator, ablation studies on different regularization techniques for the flow-based estimator and other related hyperparameters.
COST: 7920
PREDICTION: Expected results include improved fine-tuned sample quality and more rigorous enforcement of the regularized KL-regularized reward maximization objective. The effectiveness of the flow-based KL estimator could lead to over-estimation and decreased regularized KL-regularization during early stages of training, intensifying the pursuit of better adaptation in this direction.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring KL-Regularized Fine-Tuning for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of KL-regularization with different upper-bounding techniques on KL divergence between the fine-tuned distribution and the pre-trained diffusion model on text-to-image generation tasks.
CONTROLS: Run PPO with and without KL regularization, using both exact and relaxed (trajectory) KL upper-bound functions for regularization.
COST: 540
PREDICTION: We expect to see improvements in sample quality and stability when using KL regularization, but high variance in results due to the complexity of the upper-bound functions. 

This experiment will serve as a baseline for understanding the importance of KL regularization and its variants in fine-tuning diffusion models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Recovering Optimal KL Tilt via Best-of-N Sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether using Best-of-N sampling to recover the optimal KL tilt is a viable alternative for fine-tuning diffusion models, and if it can provide comparable or improved results to KL-regularized methods.
CONTROLS: Implement Best-of-N sampling instead of PPO, using the same baseline model and evaluation metrics as before, and compare its performance against KL-regularized fine-tuning.
COST: 810
PREDICTION: We expect Best-of-N sampling to offer a more efficient and stable approach to fine-tuning, but potential losses in flexibility due to its reliance on heuristics rather than KL regularization.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Leveraging Structural Information in Flow Models
PROPOSAL: - Revise Proposal 1 to investigate how incorporating structural information from the ODEs defining the flow model's reverse process into the KL-regularization scheme affects fine-tuning performance. Specifically, we will explore using the gradients of the reverse ODE to inform the KL regularization.
CONTROLS: Retain the same experiment setup as before, with the modifications that allow incorporation of ODE-based information into KL regularization.
COST: 648
PREDICTION: The integration of ODE-based information may provide a more informed and robust KL regularization scheme, potentially leading to improved stability and better capture of complex distributions.

TITLE: Revise KL-Regularized Fine-Tuning for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Revise Proposal 1 to incorporate structural information from the ODEs defining the flow model's reverse process into the KL-regularization scheme, regardless of whether the diffusion model is used or not, to investigate the broad applicability of such an approach.
CONTROLS: Run PPO with KL regularization, using both the vanilla KL upper-bound and the reformulated one that incorporates ODE-based information, on the same text-to-image generation tasks as before.

PREDICTION: The integration of ODE-based information may provide a more informed and robust KL regularization scheme, potentially leading to improved stability and better capture of complex distributions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Rejection Sampling-based Fine-Tuning for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Extend and modify Proposition 2 to investigate the fine-tuning performance of rejection sampling-based methods (e.g., RSO, RAFT, Reinforce-Rej) by applying them to diffusion models on text-to-image generation tasks.
CONTROLS: Implement RSO, RAFT, and Reinforce-Rej algorithms specifically for diffusion models and compare their performance to KL-regularized fine-tuning methods on text-to-image generation tasks.
COST: 1290
PREDICTION: Rejection sampling-based methods may provide efficient and effective fine-tuning options for diffusion models, particularly for tasks with a strong reward signal, but may struggle with adaptation to complex tasks or stable convergence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fine-Tuning Flow Models with Synthetic Data Correction
PROPOSAL: Propose an experiment to investigate whether the errors of pre-trained flow models can be corrected using only samples from the data distribution without an explicit reward, collected using a carefully designed procedure on synthetic data.
CONTROLS: Use previously-fine-tuned flow models on synthetic tasks to test if data-driven corrections can address discrepancies between the pre-trained model and the target distribution.
COST: 2100
PREDICTION: The experiment should find evidence that correction methods can retrieve closer matches to the target distribution, yet variations in initialization and batch complexity might drop calibration down.

TITLE: Model-Agnostic Multi-Task Federated Learning through Collaborative Proximal Alignment
PROPOSAL: We propose a new federated learning algorithm, referred to as Collaborative Proximal Alignment (CPA), which attempts to align the representation spaces of multiple models with different architectures and tasks through a proximal-based regularization term. Specifically, we use a centered kernel alignment-based similarity measure, but modify it to be amortized and thus not requiring explicit representation matrix diagonalization, resulting in lower computational costs. Instead, a first-order optimization-based method will be applied for each model. The weights of the models are optimized to align with other models in a proximal sense.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate CPA against three baseline methods: 
1. KGASC, which directly adds a proximal term based on centered kernel alignment, showing the limitation of requiring explicit representation matrix diagonalization. 
2. KDL, which trains task specific predictors and a shared decoder. 
3. FEDCoord, a more common approach in personalized FL. 
COST: 128000
PREDICTION: CPA should achieve significant improvements over the baselines for non-IID tasks, especially with low communication budget. TITLE: Identifying Noisy Labels through Inconsistency-based Loss
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel method that learns to identify noisy labels by leveraging the inconsistencies in the predictions of a teacher-student model, where the teacher model produces soft-labels that are used to supervise the student model. Specifically, we will train two neural networks: a teacher model with a large capacity that produces soft-labels for the training examples, and a student model with a smaller capacity that is trained to produce predictions consistent with the soft-labels. The loss for the student model will be a combination of a cross-entropy loss and an inconsistency loss, which is computed as the KL divergence between the predictions of the student model and the soft-labels produced by the teacher model. By minimizing the total loss, the student model will learn to accurately classify the clean examples and generate predictions that are inconsistent with the noisy labels, allowing us to identify the noisy labels.

PREDICTION: We expect the proposed method to outperform the baseline models and achieve state-of-the-art performance in identifying noisy labels. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Readiness of Training-Free Self-Speculative Methods for Cascades
PROPOSAL: Compare the walltime improvement of self-speculative techniques such as Lookahead, SWIFT, and BiTA with and without a retrieval-based statistical drafter, on four datasets from the machine translation and summarization domains: WMT19 En-De, WMT18 En-Fr, CNN/DM, and MSCOCO. We will use the Hugging Face Transformers library to fine-tune pre-trained models and default hyperparameters for Lookahead and SWIFT, and implement the more efficient BiTA method. Our metrics will be peak real-time, speedup factors, and space requirements, to evaluate the trade-off between added latency, walltime improvement, and extra memory usage.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard decoding; ablation: each self-speculative technique individually, combined with standard decoding rather than a retrieval-based drafter.
COST: 2500
PREDICTION: Lookahead will demonstrate significant walltime improvement, but its poor handling of context may leave SWIFT as the winner when considering summarization; BiTA's reliance on expensive matrix computations might force a careful analysis of its scalability and optimal hyperparameters; neither method, however, will outperform BiTA and a fast draft model.

Evaluated by whether cascades involving self-speculative techniques show improvements over standard speculative decoding in machine translation and summarization tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Scheduling Choices for Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: Prove or disprove whether a typical cascade configuration with fixed hyperparameters and randomly selected draft models can reach even 50% speedup over speculative decoding with a retrieval-based statistical drafter, using known assumptions about the acceptance rates and costs of self-derived draft models. Our regime will be a uniform distribution of draft model sizes across the cascade, with costs and acceptance rates following two separate power laws.
CONTROLS: Ground truth acceptance rates and costs of individual draft models will be derived from separate experiments.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: Using techniques from rate-distortion theory and optimal decision-making, we will establish a lower bound of 64% speedup when the cascade is ordered optimally, but show that fixed-hyperparameter cascades with random draft models will almost always suffer from 10-15% throughput penalty due to mischosen draft models, despite statistical convergence of optimal configurations.

TITLE: Temporally Consistent Discrete Video Tokenizers via Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose to tackle the challenge of maintaining temporal consistency in discrete video tokenizers through multi-task learning. Specifically, we add a secondary task to predict the frame-level video dynamics between adjacent frames. By training the discrete video tokenizer to jointly optimize both frame-level reconstruction and temporal consistency, the generated tokens are expected to better account for motion and contextual relationships. This proposed approach will be evaluated on the UCF-101 dataset and benchmarked using popular video quality metrics such as PSNR and SSIM.
CONTROLS: In addition to our proposed multi-task learning framework, we will maintain a baseline of regular discrete video tokenizer training, which utilizes only frame-level reconstruction as the task.

PREDICTION: We anticipate significant improvements in reconstruction quality and temporal consistency due to the additional task focusing on frame-level dynamics. However, challenge remains in striking a balance between the varying difficulties of the two tasks during training.

TITLE: Hierarchical Video Generation via View Transformer
PROPOSAL: We introduce the View Transformer, a novel framework for hierarchical video generation. The View Transformer decomposes a video into multiple views or scenes, each generated through a separate discrete autoregressive model. This hierarchical structure allows for conditioned generation and refinement of each view, improving video quality and realism. Furthermore, the View Transformer facilitates the integration of new scenes or changes into an existing video sequence, enabling more seamless video extrapolation and long-term video editing applications. We will evaluate the View Transformer on the Microsoft Holoportation dataset and LAION-400M-Full dataset.
CONTROLS: Controls will be established by comparing the proposed hierarchical framework with a traditional, non-hierarchical discrete autoregressive model on both view-level and full-sequence reconstruction metrics.

PREDICTION: We anticipate significant gains in realism and coherence of generated videos, particularly with the View Transformer's capacity for refined view generation. However, challenges remain in effectively training the hierarchical model and maintaining temporal consistency across different views.

To this end, we review recent literature on adversarial attacks in deep learning and modify these methods to accommodate the temporal nature of video generation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on various autoregressive video generators, including those using sequence-by-sequence and pixel-by-pixel methods.

TITLE: Identifying Conditions for Implication Inference in Fine-Tuned LLMs
PROPOSAL: We investigate the regime in which fine-tuned LLMs infer implications from newly injected factual knowledge. Specifically, we define a family of "connection matrices" that capture the relationships between facts and implications in the training data. By analyzing the eigenvalues of these matrices, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for the model to infer implications, which depends on the ration of the number of facts to the number of unique subjects in the training data.
CONTROLS: We compare our theory to a random baseline and an oracle that has access to the training data and the connection matrices.
COST: 1000000

PREDICTION: We expect that our theory will explain the conditions under which fine-tuned LLMs infer implications, and that the necessary and sufficient condition we derive will be sharper than the random baseline. However, we note that the oracle might outperform our theory in certain cases, particularly when the training data is too sparse. 

In future iterations, we will add additional theoretic results granting a further deeper understanding of requirement settings for implication inference, experiments over natural language processing data, and analysis under real-world scenarios, then question the surrounding effects on language processing.

This theoretical result is meant to build on the set's first proposal,  explaining why the amount of training steps can sometimes predict if a model can create implications from sentences.

TITLE: Meta-Learning for Agentic Search with Hierarchical Memory 
PROPOSAL: To tackle the challenge of scaling up agentic search to complex and dynamic environments, we propose the use of meta-learning with a hierarchical memory architecture. The meta-learner will be trained on a set of diverse search tasks, with each task represented as a hierarchical sequence of sub-goals. The hierarchical memory will be implemented as a probabilistic memory-augmented neural network (P-MANN) that can selectively access and recall relevant sub-goals at different levels of abstraction. During training, the P-MANN will be updated using a combination of self-supervised and task-supervised objectives to encourage the development of a robust and generalizable agentic search strategy. In this manner, the meta-learner will learn to adapt to new search tasks and environments by effectively combining and reusing knowledge across different levels of abstraction.

PROPOSAL: We propose to design a process reward signal that aligns with the final objective of the search agent by examining the similarity between the intermediate retrieval results and the ground-truth answer. Specifically, we calculate the cosine similarity between the sequence of search results from each intermediate turn and the final answer, and use this similarity as a dense process reward. This reward encourages the agent to engage in productive turns that effectively contribute to the final answer.

PROPOSAL: We propose to enhance the alignment-based process reward with a perception module that predicts the semantic similarity between the intermediate retrieval results and the final answer embedding. The answer embedding is a dense representation of the ground-truth answer extracted using a pre-trained language model. We aggregate the output of multiple layers of this perception module at different scales to obtain a nuanced representation of the relevance between intermediate steps and the final answer. This reward encourages the agent to engage in a more diverse range of productive turns at different scales.

TITLE: Agentic Search Reward: Multi-Scale Process Reward with Answer Embedding
PROPOSAL: We revise the previously proposed multi-scale process reward by introducing a cascading perception architecture. In each intermediate turn, the perception module receives the sequence of search results and iteratively refines its prediction of the semantic similarity with the answer embedding. TITLE: Local Exploration Rewards for Outcome-Based GRPO
PROPOSAL: Modify Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) by introducing additional process rewards that encourage exploration at each turn. Specifically, define a "local exploration bonus" (LEB) that evaluates how much new information each turn retrieves relative to its previous turn. Use this bonus to normalize outcome-based rewards within each rollout, thereby providing a dense signal that remains anchored to the final task objective. If all rollouts in a group yield identical answers, count the LEB to break ties and ensure that every rollout has a unique gradient signal. TITLE: Self-Supervised Pre-Training for Sparse Perception Models via 3D Gaussian Splatting
PROPOSAL: We propose a self-supervised pre-training method for Sparse Perception Models using 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our approach, called GSP (Gaussian Splatting Pre-training), leverages the strengths of 3D Gaussian Splatting in modeling scene geometry and texture to pre-train the sparse queries of SPMs. Specifically, we project neighboring frames onto the current frame using rendered depths and relative poses, resulting in a dense 3D scene representation. We then train the SPM to predict this 3D representation, using the rendered depths as the target output. Controls will include comparisons to different pre-training objectives (e.g., Masked Autoencoding, Contrastive Learning) and evaluations on various Sparse Perception tasks (e.g., object detection, semantic segmentation).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Adversarial Mixing Strategies for Diverse Pseudo-Label Generation
PROPOSAL: We will develop a novel pseudo-label generation method, called AMix, that employs an adversarial mixing strategy to generate high-quality pseudo-labels for vision-language detectors at test time. AMix will consist of two models: a generator network that produces a mixture of pseudo-labels from the previous batch and external knowledge from the pre-trained visual encoder, and a discriminator network that evaluates the quality of the generated pseudo-labels. The two networks will engage in a min-max game, with the generator attempting to generate pseudo-labels that are indistinguishable from the target data, and the discriminator trying to distinguish between the genuine and generated pseudo-labels. We will leverage the pre-trained visual encoder's knowledge graph to provide external information and promote diverse pseudo-labels.
CONTROLS: We will compare AMix with various baselines, including the standard self-training method, MC Dropout-based pseudo-label filtering, and a recent state-of-the-art method for pseudo-label adaptation.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: AMix will achieve superior adaptation performance compared to the baselines, especially when the pseudo-labels are noisy or missing for some test samples. However, its performance might degrade when the test data contains objects from unobserved categories in the pre-trained detector.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving Adaptation with Category-Agnostic Pseudo-Label Refining
PROPOSAL: We will propose a novel category-agnostic pseudo-label refining (CAPR) method, which can adapt vision-language detectors to new categories encountered during test-time adaptation, without the need for category-specific information. CAPR will utilize a refining network to update the pseudo-labels produced by the vision-language detector, with the goal of improving detection accuracy. The refining network will be trained to minimize a category-agnostic loss function that encourages the refined pseudo-labels to be consistent with the features from the pre-trained visual encoder. We will leverage the knowledge graph of the pre-trained visual encoder to provide valuable information for refining pseudo-labels.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate CAPR with a variety of baselines, including a standard self-training method, a pseudo-label filtering method, and a recent category-specific pseudo-label adaptation approach.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: CAPR will improve adaptation performance compared to the baselines, especially when the test data contains objects from unobserved categories in the pre-trained detector. However, its performance might suffer when the pseudo-labels are highly noisy or unreliable.

PROPOSAL: We will propose a novel method, called Adaptive KG-Embeddings, which incorporates adaptive knowledge graph embeddings to facilitate efficient test-time adaptation for vision-language detectors. We will employ a novel attention-based mechanism to selectively focus on the relevant nodes in the knowledge graph and adapt the corresponding embeddings. TITLE: Unified Geometry and Appearance Latents via Visibility-Aware Feature Fusion
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel 3D representation that jointly models geometry and appearance by fusing visibility-aware features from a foundation vision model into a unified latent space. This is achieved by training a neural network that takes as input a set of multiview images of an object and outputs a compact 3D representation that encodes both the object's shape and its view-dependent appearance. Specifically, we use a visibility-aware feature fusion mechanism that aggregates features from different views based on the visibility of their corresponding surface points, allowing us to capture view-dependent effects while preserving geometric accuracy.
CONTROLS: We compare our method against state-of-the-art geometry-only and appearance-only representations on the DTU dataset, achieving a combination of geometric and photometric accuracy that surpasses previous work. We also evaluate our method on the Princeton Shape Benchmark, demonstrating its ability to capture detailed geometry and appearance.

GeoSplash is trained using a combination of geometric reconstruction error and a novel view-dependent rendering loss function that measures the per-pixel discrepancy between rendered images and ground truth views.

TITLE: Enhanced Post-Training Quantization for VGGT: A Global-Mixing Approach
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel post-training quantization method for VGGT, where we add a global-mixing step to the quantization process. This step soft-regularizes the quantization ranges by mixing the statistics of different tokens and channels. By traversing the transformer encoder, we collect statistics for each token and channel, then apply a soft-weighted mixture to generate a new, more stable quantization range that captures the overall activation distributions of the model. We use a learned scale parameter to control the weighting, which we learn from a small calibration set. This approach directly tackles the information loss issue associated with quantized special tokens and reduces the impact of channel-wise heavy-tailed distributions.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach against standard post-training quantization (PTQ) and two widely-used quantization-aware training (QAT) methods, including Quantization-Aware Training for Transformers (QAT-T) and Filter Pruning for quantization (FPQ). We also investigate the effect of the learned scale parameter and calibration set size on our proposed method.
COST: 30000
PREDICTION: We expect our proposed global-mixing approach to yield a consistent 90% relative improvement in camera pose estimation and point map reconstruction accuracy compared to standard PTQ, and a 70% relative improvement compared to QAT-T, without incurring significant inference cost overhead.
